questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
- That there was a film and television school that accepted exchange students
- That the classes were taught in English
- That there was a combination of academic and practical film courses
- That the university was highly ranked

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had an amazing time at Boston University. The VISA application was a nightmare, so some extra help would have been much appreciated in that regard. The host university also did not organize a nice orientation week, so that was quite disappointing.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: There is this pre-departure page that BU makes where you can find a lot of information.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was an information session which was hosted by our exchange coordinator during Orientation Week.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: It is important for people to know that there is ONE person (Sage Suorsa) who is responsible for ALL the incoming exchange students at Boston University. She gets hundreds of emails each day that can easily be found online.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was horrible to find housing. It is important to know that if you want to live on campus, you will be grouped together with the freshmen, which means that you will have the last pick of accommodation. Almost all freshmen and exchange students get grouped together in Warren Towers, which is accommodation close to campus, but incredibly old. You often share a room together with other students, and for what you get you pay an insane amount.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Way more expensive than previously thought, people should really take into account how expensive it is to live in Boston. The cost of living is also really high.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The system is incredibly complicated and very old. There are several videos that you can watch and that are sent out a couple of weeks before registration, so use those to guide you through it.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It is important to know that only some courses are open for registration during the course registration period. Most courses (especially upper-level and graduate courses) require permission from either the course coordinator or the faculty. This process is INCREDIBLY slow. All the courses that I wanted to register for required pre-approval. I had to collect transcripts from both my bachelor's and master's degrees, write motivational letters, and get letters of recommendation of people who could vouch for me. I tried desperately to get everything sorted before arriving at BU, but in the end, that was not possible. Therefore, I registered for the only film courses that were open to exchange students and then changed them in the two-week add/drop period that starts at the beginning of the semester. So my advice: make a list of the courses that you wanna take that need pre-approval, and go talk to professors during the first two weeks of class. They will tell you what they need in order for you to take the class.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: This is very faculty dependent. At my faculty (Department of Communication), there was an incredibly sweet lady called Rachel who helped me register for everything. I only found her after being transferred 5 times from person to person.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: It was a struggle but in the end, I registered for all the courses that I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
- Just register for the courses that are open to exchange students
- Make a list of the courses you actually wanna register for. 
- Gather all the documents that state that you meet the prerequisites for that course (for example, I wanted to register for a course that required you to have done a course in Film Studies, so I had a course from my BA that was quite similar and attached its syllabus to my application)
- Email Sage this material, but don't expect to get admitted to the courses while being in Denmark
- Once you're at BU, talk to the professors and ask what you need to do to get admitted to these courses.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I got to follow the exact courses that I wanted to, but the level was way lower than expected.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took three 500-level courses, and I shared the classroom with juniors, seniors, and MA students.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
- The classes were smaller
- More exams and papers throughout the semester, not one big exam at the end of the semester
- Your grade is made up of several assignments 
- It's quite easy to get high grades
- Most students need to follow 4 courses, but KU students only need 3. So our workload is lower compared to other students

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- COM FT508 Line producing for undergrads
- COM FT525 Creative Producing II
- COM FT526 Feminist TV Studies

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: COM FT508 Line producing for undergrads: incredibly useful if you want to work in the film industry since they teach you how to work with MovieMagic Budgeting and Scheduling. These two programs are used throughout the entire industry, so it's very good to put on your resume and for it to be a part of your skillset.

The visa application process is incredibly expensive. Here's a breakdown:

- Sevis Fee: €205,94
- Flights to Boston: 4156 DKK (one way)
- US Visa photos: 100 DKK

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Nothing

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There is this week called SPLASH where they present all the different clubs present at the university, but they host it the third week of the semester, so quite late and not during orientation.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: A lot of different clubs, but difficult to join if you're only there for one semester

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Was not part of any

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
- Go to Salem during Halloween
- Definitely go to NYC (Flix Bus has student discounted tickets if you log in via Student Beans or UniDays)
- Visit New Haven (Yale) and Providence (Brown University)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Yes, there is not much of a culture shock between the US and DK

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: none

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Be prepared to encounter a lot of homeless people - the social system really fails in the US in this regard, and it is specifically jarring coming from Denmark, where you encounter so few.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: You can literally order anything, the supermarkets are INSANE

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Make sure you have all your vaccinations. BU requires students to have certain vaccinations that you don't automatically get vaccinated for (such as Hepatitis B and some others), so make sure in advance that you have all the required vaccines. There is also a form that needs to be signed by a doctor, so make sure that you also take care of that in advance. When I saw that we needed vaccinations as students, I assumed it was the COVID-19 vaccines, but there are a bunch of other ones. 
- As part of your application, you need to have at least $10,000 in your account or have someone (like a parent) stand as a guarantee for you. So it is important to be aware of this before you apply. 
- Check out Mint Mobile, Red Pocket, or Tello for an eSim. You can keep your Danish phone number, and pay for an American eSim which is super convenient. Share your referral code with a friend who's also studying in the States, and you'll both get a discount!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are three museums in Boston that are free to BU students, so don't pay for them!! They are: The Museum of Fine Arts, The Isabel Gardner Museum, and The Institute for Contemporary Art

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
- The academic experience
- The connections
- The new friends

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Getting into the country
- Getting the VISA
- Finding housing

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: At one point, all the Danish students that were on exchange at BU received an email stating that they were invited for a dinner with the Dean of KU. I got an email a week later, almost as an afterthought. When I responded that I wanted to join the dinner as well - just like my Danish peers - no one responded to it and it was completely ignored. All my Danish friends went, but I was the only international student there and never received a reply from the Study Abroad office nor from the office that was organizing it in Boston. The whole situation felt really shitty

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
